persons.name: Edward W. Casey
persons.note: HE HELD TWO TOWN OFFICES ACROSS THE MUNICIPAL YEAR THAT ENDED IN THE SCENE MONTH. Andreas's 1834 roster: 'Edward W. Casey, Corporation Counsel, and, from November, Clerk and Collector.' He was also one of the three men chosen for District No. 1 in the city-charter conference of November 1836, which places him in Chicago on both sides of the scene date. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Casey, Edward W.” (tax_1833_014, line 66); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Casey, Edward W.” (poll_1834_024, line 193). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Casey' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Edward Casey,” (f1839_v0123, printed page 42, ward 1, voting for John H. Kinzie). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Casey' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins E. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 2 times, as “CASEY EDWARD W”, 1833-10-24: 2 parcels of the school section — lot 5 of block 82 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 6 of block 82 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $116.00 (ls0130, ls0131). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: CASEY EDWARD W matches Edward W. Casey: the forename names Edward W. Casey of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

persons.name: J. A. Marshall
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'A. MARSHALL' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 19 November 1834, column 4. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `schoolteacher` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry. OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Marshall, James A. | 1832, | London, Eng. | 70 | Chicago.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS2A — one bearer of the surname, the forename initial agrees, and the resident's own record spells the roster's forename 'james' — the discriminator the roster's initials do not supply (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — CORROBORATION, NOT A NEW FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's fourth annual reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, held 18 May 1882, printed this man among the guests present as “Marshall, James A., 2906 Indiana avenue, Chicago.” (Chicago Tribune, 19 May 1882). The club's criterion was residence in Chicago before 1 January 1840 and majority by then: the roster therefore corroborates a pre-1840 Chicago residence and says he was alive in 1882. It gives NO year of arrival, and the address it prints is where he lived in 1882, forty-seven years after the scene date — it is not an 1835 residence and is not read as one. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS2A — one bearer of the surname, the forename initial agrees, and the resident's own record spells the roster's forename 'james' — the discriminator the roster's initials do not supply (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Marshall, Mrs. J. A. | Letter. | June 30, 1848. | Dismissed.” (second_presb_0688, printed page 193), admitted 1848-06-30 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Marshall' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins J. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a_married_womans_entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

residents.research_note: RECONSTRUCTED HOUSEHOLD — no trade recorded, in the south division, where it is counted after the re-family recorded above; it was drawn in the north division. NOBODY HERE IS NAMED BY ANY SOURCE. The 1840 Chicago schedule counts children under ten at 27% of the town and women of twenty to twenty-nine as its second-largest band; the 1835 layer the sources can name holds 15 women, because the rolls that name this town — a letter list, a voters' roll, a subscription — print men. That gap is the shape of the evidence and not a reading of the town, so the order book counts it bucket by bucket and this household is drawn against those counts. Every value on it carries the model row and the seed that redraws it, and a source naming a woman who kept her own house in this division retires the whole record. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). This household is one of the surplus the re-cut HOLDS rather than retires: the owner's ruling of 2026-09-24 re-families it into a cell the book still orders instead of un-writing it, and `refamilied` above is the whole of what that changed.
